About: Rabi oscillations of a laser-driven two-level atom on the Bloch sphere

Source

Concept
Rabi oscillations: a closed two-level atom driven by a classical laser (rotating-wave approximation, no decay) is a Bloch vector rotating rigidly about the drive axis (Ω, 0, −δ)/Ω′.
Serves
Explores how drive strength and detuning shape a driven two-level atom. The full summary unlocks when the guided inquiry is finished.
Inquiry
Predict the effect of a 1 MHz detuning before applying it, then read the cap and the effective Rabi rate off the sphere and the strip-chart.
Misconception
A widely held intuition about detuned lasers is put to the test during the inquiry — finish it to see the claim named and refuted.

Pedagogy principles applied

Predict before revealThe crux card asks whether a detuned laser still reaches P_e=1 before the cap line ever appears on the chart.
Confront the misconceptionThe crux card names the “detuning doesn’t stop it” belief, then the cap line and the shrinking trail show the flop topping out below 1.
Invariant made visibleOn resonance the axis stays in the equator and P_e always tops out at 1 — strength changes only the rate.
Operational quantitiesCap Ω²/(Ω²+δ²) and rate Ω′/2π = √(Ω²+δ²) are read live from panels tied to the sphere.
One hero sceneA rotatable Bloch sphere owns the frame; the strip-chart and energy diagram are subordinate companions.
Honest scalingThe energy diagram labels its detuning axis as magnified ×10⁸; the sphere keeps a fixed unit scale.

Guided Inquiry

1 · An arrow on a sphere

Let’s meet our atom. Its state is the gold arrow, starting at the south pole |g⟩ (ground). The pink line is the laser’s rotation axis. Press ▶ Play and watch the arrow start swinging about it.

2 · Turn up the laser

On resonance the arrow flops all the way to |e⟩ and back. Now suppose you raise the drive strength Ω/2π — what do you think changes about the swing?

3 · Strength buys speed

Let’s try it. Drag Ω/2π up and down, and watch the period stretch and shrink while the arrow still reaches |e⟩. You can read Ω′/2π in the Effective-Rabi panel as you go.

4 · Speed, not reach

Here’s why. On resonance the axis lies flat in the equator, so every turn sweeps pole to pole — P_e always tops out at 1. Strength sets only how fast, never how far.

5 · Now detune it

Now for the interesting part. Keep Ω fixed and, from resonance, detune the laser by δ/2π = 1 MHz. What do you think happens to the excited population P_e as time runs on?

6 · Watch it stall

Let’s watch it happen. Drag δ/2π toward 1 MHz: the pink axis tilts, the trail shrinks to a small circle near |g⟩, and P_e levels off under the dashed cap line. See how the laser arrow misses the upper level by ħδ in the energy diagram — the flop never reaches 1 again.

7 · Capped — and faster

So the tilted axis pins the circle below |e⟩. The Cap panel shows the ceiling: P_e can never beat Ω²/(Ω²+δ²). And the Effective-Rabi panel shows the rate: Ω′/2π = √((Ω/2π)²+(δ/2π)²) grew. Less complete, yet more frequent — a lovely twist.

8 · Why precision beats power

One last question to take away. An atomic-clock laser drifts slightly off resonance. Using what you’ve just seen, could extra laser power fix it — and what would that cost the clock?

It wins back the flop, but at a price. Raising Ω pushes the cap Ω²/(Ω²+δ²) back toward 1 because the resonance power-broadens: a strong drive can no longer tell one frequency from its neighbours. That selectivity is exactly what a clock uses to notice the drift, which is why atomic clocks and qubit gates chase resonance, not intensity.

The Physics

Rabi oscillations on the Bloch sphere · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

The state of a laser-driven two-level atom is one arrow on the Bloch sphere. This sim lets you set the laser's strength and its detuning from resonance, and shows how the arrow's path and the excited-state population Pe respond. The same picture describes a qubit, an atomic clock and a spin in an NMR magnet.

What you'll learn

  • How an atom's state becomes an arrow on a sphere, and what the laser does to that arrow.
  • How the laser strength Ω and the detuning δ together set the arrow's turning axis and turning rate.
  • How to read Pe(t): how high it can get and how often it repeats.
  • How drive strength and tuning compare as ways to excite the atom.
Where every run starts: the arrow on |g⟩, the laser axis (pink) in the equator.

What's on screen

  • State arrow (gold): the atom's state. South pole |g⟩, north pole |e⟩.
  • Laser axis (pink): the line the laser turns the arrow about.
  • Trail (teal): the arrow tip's path over the last 1¼ turns.
  • Strip-chart: Pe against time, last 10 µs. The dashed red line is the cap (section 05).
  • Energy levels: |g⟩, |e⟩ and the laser's photon energy ħωL as a pink arrow. A gap between its tip and |e⟩ is ħδ, drawn magnified ×10⁸.
  • Live readouts: Pe, the effective Rabi rate and the max population cap. The Guided Inquiry reveals them step by step.
See itRun the opening settings. Watch for: the gold arrow turning about the pink axis, with the teal trail following its tip.

Fixed: a closed two-level atom with no decay, in the rotating-wave approximation. Every run starts in |g⟩.

03

The laser turns the arrow about an axis

A pure state is a unit arrow b = (bx, by, bz). Its height gives the population, Pe = (1 + bz)/2, so Pe = 0 at the south pole |g⟩ and 1 at the north pole |e⟩. In the frame that rotates with the laser, and keeping only the near-resonant part of the field, the drive is constant:

Ω is the drive strength and δ = ωL − ω₀ the detuning: the two sliders.

A constant drive turns the arrow rigidly about a fixed axis n̂ at angular rate Ω′, starting from |g⟩. Section 04 gives n̂ and Ω′.

One rigid rotation, always from the ground state.

On resonance (δ = 0), n̂ lies along x in the equator and Ω′ = Ω. The arrow then runs along a great circle through both poles: it reaches |e⟩ and returns once per turn. At Ω/2π = 0.5 MHz a turn takes 1/(0.5 MHz) = 2 µs, with Pe = 1 first at 1 µs. Changing Ω changes the turning rate and nothing else.

Key idea. Driving the atom means turning its arrow. Pe is only the height of the tip, which is what the strip-chart plots.
See itStay on resonance and set Ω/2π to 2 MHz. Watch for: the chart's peaks still touching 1, now four times as often as at 0.5 MHz.
04

Detuning tips the axis

Off resonance, the axis leaves the equator and the turning rate grows:

The axis n̂ and its tilt θ above the equator (negative means below).
Ω′ is never smaller than Ω.
  • Tilt. θ = 0 at δ = 0. For δ > 0 the +x end of the axis dips below the equator, and for δ < 0 it rises above. θ depends only on the ratio δ/Ω.
  • Path. The arrow still starts at |g⟩, which is now off the axis, so it circles the axis on a circle through |g⟩ of radius Ω/Ω′. The more tilted the axis, the smaller the circle.
  • Reach. That circle passes through |e⟩ only if |e⟩ and |g⟩ are equally far from the axis, which needs the axis in the equator. For δ ≠ 0 the arrow never reaches |e⟩.
See itDetune by δ/2π = 1 MHz at Ω/2π = 0.5 MHz. Watch for: the pink axis tipping, and the teal trail shrinking to a small circle near |g⟩.
05

The ceiling and the rate of Pe

Reading the height of the tip off the turning motion gives the strip-chart's curve:

One factor sets how high, the other how often.
The dashed cap line on the chart.
  • Ceiling. The first factor is the cap, the square of the circle's radius Ω/Ω′.
  • Rate. The sin² factor repeats every 2π/Ω′, which is 1/(Ω′/2π) in time. Pe first peaks at half of that.
  • Opposite trends. As |δ| grows, Ω′ grows: the cap falls and the rate rises.

06

A stronger drive widens the resonance

At fixed Ω the cap depends only on δ: Pemax = 1/(1 + (δ/Ω)²). It is a peak of height 1 and half-width Ω, falling to ½ at |δ| = Ω.

  • Strength widens the peak and leaves its top at 1. At δ/2π = 1 MHz the cap is 0.20 for Ω/2π = 0.5 MHz and 0.80 for 2 MHz. At δ = 0 it is 1 for both.
  • A narrow peak is selective. Keeping the cap above 0.99 needs |δ| ≤ Ω/√99 ≈ 0.1 Ω, which is 50 kHz at Ω/2π = 0.5 MHz. A wider peak forgives more detuning but responds less sharply to a small frequency error. Spectroscopists call this widening by a stronger probe power broadening.
See itHold δ/2π = 1 MHz and compare Ω/2π = 0.5 MHz with 2 MHz. Watch for: the cap readout, and the dashed line on the chart, rising from 0.200 to 0.800.
07

Where it matters

  • Qubit gates. Any two-level system, such as a superconducting or trapped-ion qubit, obeys these equations. A resonant drive lasting π/Ω turns |g⟩ into |e⟩, and a detuned one falls short. The sim keeps the drive on, so Pe first peaks at π/Ω and the arrow keeps turning.
  • Atomic clocks and spectroscopy. A laser is tuned to an atomic resonance. The narrower the response to δ, the better a small drift shows, and a strong probe broadens the line it measures.
  • NMR and MRI. A spin driven by a radio-frequency field follows the same rotation. It tips fully only on resonance, which MRI uses to excite a chosen slice.
Go deeper: the rotating frame and the closed-form solution
The three components the sim evaluates every frame. No numerical integration is involved.
  • The sphere is drawn in the frame turning at the laser frequency. The part of the field that nearly matches the atom becomes the constant drive above. The rest oscillates at about twice the transition frequency and averages out: the rotating-wave approximation, excellent when Ω and δ are MHz and the transition is near 400 THz.
  • bz is the population difference; bx and by carry the phase relative to the laser.
  • Nothing decays here, so the oscillation never dies down. A real atom also decays and dephases.
08

Summary

In one line. The laser turns the atom's Bloch arrow about a fixed axis at rate Ω′; detuning tips that axis, which lowers the ceiling on Pe and raises the rate.

Key points

  • Pe = (1 + bz)/2 is the height of the arrow's tip.
  • The axis is (Ω, 0, −δ)/Ω′ and the turning rate is Ω′ = √(Ω² + δ²).
  • Pe peaks at Ω²/(Ω² + δ²) once every 1/(Ω′/2π).
  • Only δ = 0 reaches |e⟩. A stronger drive widens the resonance, not its top.

Common mix-ups

  • "A stronger laser excites the atom more." On resonance the flop is already complete, so Ω sets only the rate. Off resonance it raises the cap, which still reaches 1 only at δ = 0.
  • "Detuned, the atom still reaches |e⟩; it just takes longer." It never does, and the oscillation gets faster, not slower.
  • "Red and blue detuning behave differently." Pe depends on δ², so ±δ give the same cap and rate. Only the direction of the tilt, and the sign of bx, flip.

Things to try on your own

  • At Ω/2π = 0.5 MHz, find the largest δ/2π, in steps of 0.05 MHz, with the cap at least 0.9. Repeat at 1 MHz and compare with Ω/3.
  • Choose Ω and δ so the cap is about 0.5 and one turn takes about 1 µs.
  • Set δ/2π = +1 MHz, then −1 MHz. Compare the cap, the rate and the lean of the trail.
